name: Wichita
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Wichita, KS | Genstone
metaDescription: Wichita investor rehabs for aircraft-era ranches, College Hill Tudors and Riverside foursquares: pre-offer reviews, hail-ready scopes, draws by work.
intro:
Wichita’s housing was built by the aircraft industry. Waves of hiring at the plants that made the city the Air Capital filled whole quadrants with modest ranches and wartime cottages, and those houses now make up a large share of what investors buy, renovate and rent here. Layer on older College Hill, Riverside and Midtown homes, a busy hail season and a joint city-county building department, and you have a market that rewards contractors who know it.

Genstone Construction renovates investment homes for individual investors, funds, lenders, servicers and Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We are headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and in Wichita our work is carried out by vetted, licensed and insured local contractors that a single designated field manager coordinates on your behalf. A free Pre-Offer Rehab Review comes first, pricing the repairs and refining your after-repair value so you know whether the purchase price works. Next comes a written scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule. Permits and inspections run through the Metropolitan Area Building and Construction Department, payment follows completed work rather than preceding it, and debris removal is in the estimate from the start.
housingStock:
The oldest neighborhoods hug the Arkansas River and downtown. Riverside, Midtown and Delano carry late-1800s and early-1900s Victorians, foursquares and frame cottages, many on stone or brick foundations with partial basements or cellars. College Hill and Crown Heights, to the east, developed in the 1910s through 1930s with brick Tudors, Colonial Revivals and well-built bungalows, and they remain some of the most sought-after older homes in the city. Fairmount, around Wichita State University, mixes bungalows with houses long since converted to student rentals.

The defining layer, though, is aircraft-era housing. During the Second World War, Planeview was built in a hurry to house workers at the Boeing plant, and Hilltop Manor went up for the same reason. After the war, ranches spread across the south, east and west sides for families tied to the plants and to McConnell Air Force Base. Many are small frame or brick-veneer houses on full or partial basements, with simple roof lines and modest kitchens.

From the 1960s onward, development pushed farther east and west toward Andover, Maize and Goddard, adding split-levels, larger ranches and two-stories with finished basements.

What that means for a rehab: expect older electrical in the pre-war and wartime houses, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains in mid-century ranches, asbestos in some 1950s and 1960s flooring and duct materials, and lead paint in anything built before 1978. Basement walls built from block or poured concrete can crack and bow where clay soils swell and shrink, and nearly every roof in the city will be judged by how it has held up to hail. Low-lying homes near the river and the old creek channels also deserve a check of flood history, since the floodway that diverts water around the city did not remove every wet spot.

commonIssues.title: Hail-worn roofs, siding and gutters
commonIssues.body: Wichita sits in one of the most active hail corridors in the country, and many houses have had more than one roof. Investors frequently buy homes with dented gutters, cracked vinyl siding, bruised shingles and roof decking that has been layered over rather than replaced. Insurers and buyers both care about roof age and condition. We look at the roof from the attic as well as the outside, and we price tear-off, decking repair and siding replacement as separate lines.

commonIssues.title: Basement wall movement in clay soil
commonIssues.body: Parts of Wichita sit on clay that swells when wet and shrinks during drought, and the long hot summers followed by heavy spring rain work basement walls hard. Horizontal cracks, inward bowing and stair-step cracking in block walls are common in mid-century ranches. Some movement is cosmetic; some requires bracing, anchors or wall rebuilding. We evaluate walls carefully and recommend an engineer when bowing is significant, because this one item can reshape a budget.

commonIssues.title: Wartime and post-war electrical
commonIssues.body: Planeview, Hilltop and many early post-war ranches were built quickly and economically, and their electrical systems reflect it: small services, two-prong ungrounded circuits, undersized wiring and decades of owner additions. Insurers often balk at older panels, and buyers’ inspectors flag them. Most of these houses need a new service and panel and at least partial rewiring, which is usually simpler in drywall-and-paneling ranches than in plaster homes, but still needs to be completed and inspected before finishes.

commonIssues.title: Old drain and supply piping
commonIssues.body: Galvanized steel supply lines and cast-iron drain lines are standard in Wichita houses built before the mid-1960s, and clay or cast-iron sewer laterals run from many of them to the main. Galvanized pipe rusts internally and restricts flow; cast iron cracks and corrodes under basement slabs. We recommend a camera inspection of the main drain and lateral before closing, and we price repiping and slab work separately so you can see their effect on your numbers.

commonIssues.title: Converted and divided houses
commonIssues.body: Near Wichita State and in older central neighborhoods, some houses were divided into apartments or rented by the room with little regard for code. That can mean shared utilities, missing fire separation, bedrooms without egress windows and stairs that do not meet current standards. Before you buy one, we look at how it was configured and what it would take either to legalize the arrangement or to return the house to single-family use.

investorMarket:
Wichita has long attracted out-of-state rental investors because purchase prices are modest and a large share of the housing stock is simple, solid ranches that rent well. The strategy that fits best depends heavily on which side of town you are in.

Flips work most reliably in College Hill, Crown Heights, Riverside and the established east-side neighborhoods, where owner-occupants pay for character, good schools and proximity to employers, and in newer subdivisions toward Andover and Maize. Buyers in College Hill expect careful work on brick, trim and hardwood; buyers on the east side want open kitchens and finished basements.

Rental and BRRRR investors concentrate on the south and west sides, in areas such as Planeview, Hilltop, South Central and the neighborhoods near the aircraft plants and McConnell, where purchase prices are lower and demand from working households is steady. Those houses are often small, so adding a bathroom or a legal basement bedroom can matter more than finishes.

Small multifamily is spread across Fairmount and Midtown, where older houses were converted, and across east and west Wichita, where purpose-built duplexes and fourplexes from the 1970s and 1980s are common. Bank-owned and servicer-held homes appear across the city, particularly in older post-war neighborhoods, often with hail damage, deferred maintenance and basement water problems.
permits:
Building permits in Wichita and unincorporated Sedgwick County are handled by the Metropolitan Area Building and Construction Department, a joint city-county agency that reviews plans, issues permits and conducts inspections. The same department licenses contractors working in its jurisdiction, so general and trade contractors need the appropriate license before they can pull permits.

Structural repairs, basement wall stabilization, additions, decks, new or altered electrical, plumbing and mechanical systems, and most water heater and furnace replacements require permits. Roof replacements and siding work may also need permits depending on scope, and we confirm the requirement for each job. Inspections occur at rough-in and final stages, and we schedule them so walls and ceilings can be closed without delay.

Properties in the Arkansas River floodplain or near the floodway may be subject to additional review for substantial improvements. Surrounding cities such as Derby, Andover and Haysville may run their own building processes or contract with others, and requirements vary. Genstone confirms the jurisdiction for every address, prepares applications, coordinates inspections and collects lien waivers throughout the project.
climate:
Wichita’s weather is hard on houses. Summers are hot and often dry, winters are cold and windy, and spring delivers some of the most severe hail and thunderstorm activity in the country. Large hail damages roofs, siding, gutters and windows, and strong straight-line winds and occasional tornadoes add to the toll.

The swing between drought and heavy rain stresses basement walls and foundations in clay soils, and intense spring storms reveal poor grading and failing sump systems quickly. Ice storms occasionally knock out power for extended periods, which can freeze pipes in a vacant house.

We schedule roofing and exterior work outside the worst storm windows when possible, keep vacant homes heated or winterized, and prioritize drainage and grading corrections alongside basement repairs. Air conditioning is essential in summer, so HVAC is typically sequenced early on hot-weather projects.

faqs.q: Do you replace hail-damaged roofs as part of a rehab?
faqs.a: Yes. Roof and exterior work is part of many Wichita scopes because hail is so frequent. We inspect the roof from inside the attic and outside, price tear-off and decking repairs, and include siding, gutters and window screens where hail has damaged them. If an insurance claim is involved, we provide documentation of conditions and completed work for your records.

faqs.q: Is a contractor license required in Wichita?
faqs.a: Yes. The Metropolitan Area Building and Construction Department licenses contractors working in Wichita and unincorporated Sedgwick County, and permits are pulled by appropriately licensed contractors. Genstone coordinates licensed local contractors for every project, so permitted work is performed and inspected properly. That matters for resale, insurance and refinancing, where unpermitted work can create problems. License status is also something a buyer’s agent or lender may ask about during a sale.

faqs.q: Do you work in Derby, Andover and Haysville?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate contractors across the Wichita metro, including Derby, Haysville, Andover, Park City, Bel Aire and Maize. Permitting and inspection processes vary by city, so we confirm requirements for each address and write the scope accordingly. Newer housing in those communities often needs lighter work than central Wichita homes, which affects both pricing and scheduling. One field manager still oversees every address, inside or outside the city.

faqs.q: What does the Pre-Offer Rehab Review include?
faqs.a: It is a free assessment before you commit to a purchase. We walk the property, estimate repair costs, refine your after-repair value and tell you whether the numbers support your offer. In Wichita we pay close attention to roof condition, basement walls, electrical panels, drain lines and any signs of past water intrusion, because those are the items most likely to change your budget.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Wichita, KS | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Wichita flip renovations in College Hill, Riverside and east-side ranches: roof, basement and panel work priced first, finishes matched to comps.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Wichita
fix-flip.intro: Wichita flips usually take one of two shapes. On one side are College Hill, Crown Heights and Riverside homes, where buyers pay for brick, hardwood and old-house character. On the other are mid-century ranches across the east and west sides, where buyers want open kitchens, updated baths and finished basements at a price that fits a household budget. Both kinds of buyer will have an inspector look hard at the roof, the basement walls and the electrical panel. Genstone Construction prices those items during a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review and refines your after-repair value against the renovated comps nearby. Your scope often includes two finish levels so you can compare margin, and a designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, permits and inspections through MABCD while you track progress remotely. Draws are tied to completed work with no upfront payment.

sections.h2: Finishes that match each Wichita neighborhood
sections.body:
In College Hill and Crown Heights, flips succeed by respecting the house. Buyers there walk in expecting refinished oak floors, intact trim, working fireplaces and kitchens that look current without fighting the architecture. Pulling out original built-ins or covering hardwood with vinyl can make those homes harder to sell at the top of the comp range.

Riverside and Midtown buyers are similar but often more price-sensitive, and they will accept a simpler kitchen if the house has character and sound systems. In the post-war ranch belts on the east and west sides, buyers compare your house to several other renovated ranches nearby, so clean modern finishes, a second bathroom where possible and a finished, dry basement can make a real difference.

We write each scope against the comps you are using. When the finish decision is close, we price two options side by side, such as painted original cabinets versus a new kitchen layout, so you can see which one is likely to return its cost in that specific part of Wichita.

sections.h2: Roof, basement and panel before paint
sections.body:
Wichita buyers’ inspectors know the local trouble spots. They look closely at roof age and hail damage, basement wall cracks and bowing, signs of past water intrusion, and the age and brand of the electrical panel. A flip that skips any of those risks a renegotiation or a buyer walking away.

We price those items first. That often means a full roof tear-off with decking repair, new gutters and sometimes new siding; basement wall evaluation, with bracing or anchors where bowing is significant, along with grading corrections and a working sump where needed; and a new electrical service and panel with grounded circuits.

Plumbing follows close behind. Mid-century ranches commonly have galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains, and a camera inspection of the main and lateral before closing often saves an expensive surprise. Completing and permitting that work before cosmetics begin protects your sale price and gives the buyer’s inspector little to argue about.

sections.h2: Timing a Wichita flip around storm season
sections.body:
Carrying costs add up quickly on a flip, and in Wichita the weather is often the biggest schedule risk. Spring storms can delay roofing and exterior work, and a hail event can tie up roofing crews across the city for weeks afterward. We plan exterior work outside the worst windows when we can, and we order roofing materials and windows early to avoid shortages after a major storm.

Interior work continues regardless of weather. We sequence electrical, plumbing and HVAC rough-ins quickly, schedule MABCD inspections promptly and close walls without waiting. Your field manager posts progress photos and milestone updates, so you can follow the job without being on site and coordinate your listing date with your agent.

If you financed the purchase with a Genstone Financial fix-and-flip loan, the draw schedule in our scope aligns with the way that lender releases funds, which keeps cash flow predictable throughout the project.

faqs.q: Which Wichita neighborhoods do you flip in?
faqs.a: Our flip projects most often fall in College Hill, Crown Heights, Riverside, Midtown and the established east side, along with post-war ranch neighborhoods on the west side and newer subdivisions toward Andover and Maize. The right choice depends on your budget and the comps available. We help you compare the renovation a house needs with what renovated homes nearby have sold for.

faqs.q: Will buyers care about the age of the roof?
faqs.a: Very much so. In Wichita, roof age and hail damage are among the first things buyers, inspectors and insurers look at. A new roof with documentation is a strong selling point, while an older or damaged roof often leads to repair requests or price reductions. We include roof condition in every flip scope we prepare, and we keep the permit and material records so your agent can show buyers exactly when it was replaced.

faqs.q: Do you finish basements on flips?
faqs.a: Yes, when the walls are sound and dry. In Wichita ranches, a finished basement with a legal bedroom and bathroom can add meaningful value. We address wall movement, drainage and egress first, then frame, insulate and finish the space with moisture-tolerant materials so it holds up after the sale. Buyers’ inspectors check basements closely in Wichita, so a permitted, dry and properly finished lower level tends to inspect cleanly.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Wichita, KS | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Wichita BRRRR rehabs on aircraft-era ranches and cottages: renovations aimed at the refinance appraisal, hail-resistant exteriors, durable interiors.
brrrr.intro: Wichita has been a favorite BRRRR market for years, in large part because the city’s aircraft-era ranches can be bought, renovated and rented at numbers that still work. Steady demand from aerospace, healthcare and McConnell Air Force Base households keeps those houses leased. The plan only succeeds, however, if the refinance appraisal supports your numbers and the house holds up through years of tenants and hailstorms. Genstone Construction scopes Wichita BRRRR projects for both. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks at the comparable sales an appraiser is likely to use and prices the roof, basement and mechanical work that protects your cash flow. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, permits go through MABCD, and draws follow completed work. When you reach the refinance stage, Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans.

sections.h2: Appraisals on Wichita’s south and west sides
sections.body:
BRRRR investors in Wichita tend to buy on the south and west sides, in neighborhoods such as Planeview, Hilltop, South Central and the post-war tracts near the aircraft plants. Purchase prices there are lower, but renovated comparable sales can be limited, and an appraiser may have to reach across a busy street or into a different housing type to find them.

Before you buy, we look at the renovated sales an appraiser is likely to use and what features they had. Then we scope the house to match them in the items that count: updated kitchens and bathrooms, a newer roof, modern electrical and HVAC, and in many cases an added bedroom or bathroom. Small two-bedroom ranches and wartime cottages often gain more from an added bath or a legal basement bedroom than from any finish upgrade.

We document each improvement with photos, permits and lien waivers so you can provide a clear list to the appraiser and lender. That is particularly important for improvements that are not obvious during a walkthrough, such as new wiring, drain lines or basement wall stabilization.

sections.h2: Materials for a long Wichita hold
sections.body:
After the refinance, every renovation choice becomes either a durable asset or a maintenance cost. For Wichita rentals, the exterior deserves particular attention. Impact-resistant shingles, sturdier gutters and siding that tolerates hail can reduce the frequency of exterior repairs during a long hold, and they may affect insurance terms as well.

Inside, we favor luxury vinyl plank over carpet in main living areas, scrubbable paint, durable counters and common fixtures with parts available locally. Basement finishes, where used, should be moisture-tolerant, with proper drainage and a working sump if the property needs one.

Mechanical systems matter just as much. Replacing galvanized supply lines, updating the electrical service and installing properly sized HVAC reduce emergency calls, especially during hot summers, when a failed air conditioner becomes an urgent tenant issue. When the budget cannot cover everything, we rank the items by how much they protect the property over the hold, so the cosmetic extras are the first to go.

A Wichita BRRRR property should be ready for tenants on day one: working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, safe electrical with grounded outlets and GFCI protection, sound stairs and handrails, reliable heat and air, secure doors and windows, and no leaks or moisture problems. Building to that standard during the renovation is far cheaper than responding to complaints after the lease starts.

Basement bedrooms deserve care. To count as legal bedrooms, and to be safe for tenants, they need egress windows of the proper size and window wells that drain correctly. We scope those openings with the basement wall condition in mind, because cutting a new window into a cracked or bowing wall requires structural attention.

If your property is in a nearby city such as Haysville or Derby, local requirements may differ from those in Wichita. We confirm which rules apply during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the scope and schedule reflect the inspections the house will actually face.

faqs.q: Are Planeview and Hilltop houses good BRRRR candidates?
faqs.a: Some are. These wartime neighborhoods offer low purchase prices and steady rental demand, but the houses are small, the construction was economical and comparable renovated sales can be limited. The key question is whether the refinance value will support your plan. We look at that during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, along with the electrical and plumbing work these homes usually need.

faqs.q: Can impact-resistant shingles help a rental?
faqs.a: Often. In Wichita, where hail is frequent, impact-resistant shingles can reduce roof damage over a long hold and may influence insurance terms, depending on your carrier. They cost more upfront, so we price them alongside standard shingles in your scope. That way you can decide whether the long-term benefit is worth it for that property. Ask your insurance agent about the rating before you choose.

faqs.q: Do you provide documentation for my refinance?
faqs.a: Yes. We provide the scope, before and after photos, permit records and lien waivers. Wichita investors use that package to show appraisers and lenders what was done, especially for improvements behind walls or in basements. If Genstone Financial handles your DSCR refinance, its reviewers work from that same file. Closed MABCD permits also keep the title review from stalling on open work.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Wichita, KS | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Wichita single-family rental renovations and turns: portfolio standards for ranches and cottages, hail-ready exteriors, durable interiors, one manager.
rental-renovation.intro: Single-family rentals are a cornerstone of Wichita’s housing market. Many are modest post-war ranches and wartime cottages on the south and west sides; others are larger homes on the east side or older houses in Midtown and Fairmount. Owners range from local landlords to out-of-state investors and funds holding portfolios across the city. Genstone Construction renovates and turns Wichita rentals with a designated field manager, licensed local contractors and consistent written standards, so each house meets the same expectations no matter which neighborhood it is in. Every scope lists labor, materials and a draw schedule, permits are pulled through MABCD when required, and each job is documented with photos. Genstone Field Services adds make-ready, inspection and occupied maintenance support.

sections.h2: A portfolio standard for Wichita houses
sections.body:
Owners with several Wichita rentals benefit from a written standard: the same flooring, paint colors, fixtures and appliance package at every address, so repairs and turns use parts already on hand and tenants receive a consistent product. We help owners set that standard and then apply it across the city’s main housing types.

Wartime cottages in Planeview and Hilltop are small, often on slabs or crawlspaces, and may need electrical work and bathroom updates. Post-war ranches usually have basements that need to be kept dry and safe, along with original plumbing that may need replacement. Newer east and west side homes have simpler needs but more square footage to maintain.

We adapt the standard to each house while keeping pricing consistent, so you can compare costs across the portfolio. Items outside the standard, such as roof replacement, basement wall repairs or a new electrical service, are listed separately so you can plan capital spending and track the performance of each property over time.

sections.h2: Turns that hold up to tenants and hail
sections.body:
A good Wichita turn reduces calls during the next lease. In addition to the interior checklist, we look at the roof and gutters for storm damage, check window screens and siding, confirm the sump pump works and look for signs of water in the basement. Those are the items that tend to cause problems once a new tenant is in place.

Inside, we repair walls and repaint with washable finishes, replace damaged carpet with luxury vinyl plank where it makes sense, re-caulk tubs and showers, and service the furnace and air conditioning. Summer heat in Wichita makes a working AC a priority, so we test cooling before move-in.

Tenant damage is documented separately from normal wear with photographs to support your security deposit decisions. We schedule turns to minimize vacancy, and in winter we keep the heat on in vacant homes so supply lines are protected during cold snaps and ice storms.

Not every repair can wait for a vacancy. Through Genstone Field Services, we coordinate maintenance at occupied Wichita rentals: scheduling access with tenants, protecting belongings, keeping work areas safe and finishing efficiently. That includes common requests such as water heater replacements, HVAC repairs, plumbing leaks and electrical problems.

After a major hailstorm, portfolio owners often need many properties inspected and repaired at once. We can help assess damage across multiple addresses, document conditions for insurance purposes and schedule repairs in a sensible order, starting with properties where roof damage threatens interior finishes.

Our documentation of each job, including photos and descriptions of completed work, gives you a reliable maintenance history for every property. That record helps with insurance claims, tenant disputes, property management transitions and decisions about when to sell or refinance a particular house in the portfolio.

The Wichita storm season also argues for keeping basic exterior maintenance on a schedule. Cleaning gutters before spring, checking sump pumps and trimming limbs over roofs are inexpensive tasks that prevent many of the claims landlords file after a big storm.

faqs.q: Can you inspect several rentals after a hailstorm?
faqs.a: Yes. We can coordinate inspections across multiple Wichita properties, document damage with photos and prioritize repairs based on the risk of interior water damage. That documentation can support insurance claims, and the repair scopes are priced consistently so you can plan spending across the portfolio rather than reacting one property at a time. Houses with active leaks are scheduled first.

faqs.q: Do you handle rentals outside Wichita city limits?
faqs.a: Yes. We work across the metro, including Derby, Haysville, Park City, Bel Aire, Maize and other surrounding communities. Permitting requirements vary, so we confirm the rules for each address. A house in Maize or Haysville is held to the same finish standard, pricing method and photo documentation as one in central Wichita, so your portfolio reports compare cleanly from one quarter to the next.

faqs.q: What does the workmanship warranty cover?
faqs.a: Completed Wichita rental work carries Genstone’s one-year workmanship warranty. That covers defects in how we installed something, such as a leaking supply connection or a door that was hung poorly. It does not extend to damage caused by tenants or to normal wear and tear. Because each job is photographed and itemized, it is straightforward to confirm what was installed, by which trade and on what date.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and Fourplex Renovation in Wichita, KS | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Wichita duplex and fourplex renovations: 1970s–80s buildings, converted homes near Wichita State, shared roofs and systems, phased occupied work.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Fourplex Renovations in Wichita
multifamily-renovation.intro: Wichita’s small multifamily stock falls into two broad groups. Purpose-built duplexes and fourplexes, many from the 1970s and 1980s, line streets on the east and west sides and near major corridors. Older houses in Fairmount, Midtown and Riverside have been converted into two, three or four units over the decades, often to serve Wichita State students and downtown workers. Each group comes with its own shared-system questions and its own code history. Genstone Construction renovates two-to-four-unit buildings across Wichita with unit-by-unit scopes, building-wide items priced separately and phasing for occupied buildings. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, permits and inspections run through MABCD, and draws follow completed work with no upfront payment.

sections.body:
The duplexes and fourplexes built across east and west Wichita in the 1970s and 1980s are usually straightforward buildings: slab or basement foundations, separate meters and HVAC for each unit, a shared roof and simple layouts. Their age, however, means many systems are at or past the end of their life.

Typical needs include replacing original or second-generation furnaces and air conditioners, water heaters, aluminum or early vinyl windows and builder-grade kitchens and baths. Roofs on these buildings have often been through several hailstorms, and siding and gutters may need replacement. Parking areas and sidewalks can also be part of the scope.

We write these projects with a repeatable unit package, so each unit receives the same finishes and fixtures. That simplifies purchasing, speeds the work and makes future turns easier. Building-wide items are listed separately from unit interiors so you can see what the shell costs and plan capital spending, which also helps when you present the project to a lender or partner.

In Fairmount, Midtown and Riverside, many small multifamily buildings began as large single-family homes. Conversions from earlier decades can include shared electrical services, a single water heater for several units, plumbing that runs through other apartments, and exterior stairs that serve as the only access to upper units.

Before you buy, we review whether the unit count appears to be legal and how utilities are arranged, and we flag issues such as inadequate fire separation, missing second exits and bedrooms without egress. Separating utilities, adding fire-rated assemblies and rebuilding stairs can be significant expenses, but they make the building safer, easier to insure and more attractive to lenders and buyers.

These older buildings also share the central neighborhoods’ typical issues: older wiring, galvanized plumbing, basement water and lead paint. We price that work alongside the unit interiors so the full cost is visible before you commit to the purchase. Fairmount buildings in particular have often been through several owners and rounds of patching.

sections.h2: Working around tenants and the school year
sections.body:
Wichita multifamily buildings often change hands with some units occupied. We phase work so vacant units are finished first, then move to occupied units as leases end or tenants relocate within the building. Building-wide projects such as roof replacement, siding, main water lines or electrical service upgrades are scheduled with advance notice to tenants and with shutoffs kept short.

Near Wichita State, leases often turn over in late spring and summer, so the most intensive unit work is concentrated then, allowing units to be ready for fall. Exterior work can continue during the school year with careful attention to access and safety.

Your field manager coordinates tenant access, keeps common areas clean and safe and posts progress updates so you can report to partners or lenders. Each unit is documented before and after renovation, which supports future turns, insurance questions and the eventual sale of the building. Storm-related exterior work is scheduled with the forecast in mind.

faqs.q: Should I renovate all units in a fourplex at once?
faqs.a: When the units are vacant, renovating them together is usually the most efficient approach, because crews, materials and inspections can be coordinated across the building. When some units are occupied, we phase the work. Either way, we use a consistent unit package so the building is easier to manage, lease and value. Appraisers also find a uniform building simpler to compare against other Wichita fourplexes.

faqs.q: Can you separate utilities in a converted house?
faqs.a: Yes. Separating electrical services, water heaters and heating systems lets tenants pay their own utilities and can make the building easier to finance and sell. In older Wichita conversions, this can be a substantial scope item, so we price it separately and let you weigh it against the expected improvement in income. The existing service may need an upgrade before it can be split.

faqs.q: Do you handle roof and siding replacement on multifamily buildings?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Wichita duplexes and fourplexes have hail-damaged roofs, siding and gutters. We scope and price exterior replacement as a building-wide item, coordinate licensed contractors and manage permits. We also schedule the work to keep tenants safe and minimize disruption to occupied units. When an insurance claim is open, we document conditions so the adjuster and owner see the same picture, and we can price impact-resistant shingles as an option.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203k Contractor in Wichita, KS | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor for Wichita buyers, agents and lenders: itemized bids for ranches and older homes, consultant coordination, draws.
fha-203k.intro: Wichita’s supply of modest older homes makes it well suited to the FHA 203(k) program. A buyer can purchase a dated post-war ranch, a College Hill bungalow that needs systems work or a Riverside foursquare with an aging roof and finance the improvements in one mortgage. What slows these loans down is rarely the house; it is a contractor who has never handled the paperwork. Genstone holds FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status, and our Wichita bids are written in the itemized form consultants and underwriters expect. We coordinate with the HUD consultant on Standard loans, pull permits through MABCD, line up inspections and send each draw request with photos and lien waivers attached. The buyer deals with a single field manager, the agent sees the file keep moving toward closing, and the lender gets paperwork that does not need to be sent back.

sections.body:
Most Wichita 203(k) files start as a Limited loan question. That version is capped at $75,000 and excludes structural repairs, and it comfortably handles the typical east or west side ranch scope: tear-off roof, furnace and air conditioner, a panel change, a kitchen and bath refresh, flooring and paint. Once the work turns structural or grows larger, the Standard 203(k) applies, and a HUD-approved consultant joins the file. Genstone’s own program materials reference a $5,000 minimum repair amount and a $15,000 inspection threshold.

In this city, the basement usually settles the question. A block wall bowing inward from clay pressure needs bracing, anchors or partial rebuilding, and that is structural. So is cutting a new egress opening in a foundation wall to create a basement bedroom, which many buyers of small two-bedroom ranches want.

We go down the basement stairs early in every walkthrough for that reason. Knowing whether the wall work is coming lets the loan officer set up the right program at application, instead of discovering it at appraisal and restarting a file the buyer has already waited on.

sections.h2: Wichita homes that fit the program
sections.body:
Good 203(k) candidates in Wichita include post-war ranches on the east and west sides that need roofs, HVAC, electrical and kitchen and bath updates; College Hill and Crown Heights homes with sound structure but dated systems; and Riverside and Midtown houses with character but deferred maintenance. Many of these homes would struggle to pass a standard FHA appraisal as-is, which is where the 203(k) helps.

FHA also allows owner-occupants to purchase two-to-four-unit properties, so Wichita duplexes and fourplexes can work for buyers who plan to live in one unit and rent the others.

Houses with severe basement movement, major unpermitted additions or extensive storm damage can be harder to fit within loan limits and appraised value. A quick read from us before the buyer orders an appraisal can tell everyone whether a specific Wichita property is realistic for the program.

Hail history is worth asking about too. A house that has had a roof claim paid but never repaired can carry a scope larger than it looks from the street, and that money has to fit inside the loan.

Wichita underwriters and consultants send back bids that lump work together, so ours break each item into labor and material lines that track the consultant’s write-up item by item. We mark which lines need an MABCD permit and add the FHA minimum property items an appraiser will look for in an older house: flaking paint on anything built before 1978, absent handrails, active roof leaks and heat that does not run.

Once the loan closes, the repair escrow pays out in stages tied to inspected progress. Every request we submit carries dated photos, a plain description of what was finished and lien waivers from the trades paid in that stage. Hidden conditions behind paneling or under a basement slab are photographed and sent up as a change order, and that work waits for approval.

Buyers in these files are often carrying rent and a mortgage at once, which makes every idle week expensive. Our field manager books MABCD inspections ahead of need, keeps trades stacked so the house is never sitting empty, and sends the buyer, agent and loan officer the same weekly status.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan cover a new roof in Wichita?
faqs.a: Yes. Roof replacement is one of the most common items in Wichita 203(k) scopes, given how often hail damages roofs here. A roof replacement alone may fit within a Limited 203(k), along with other non-structural repairs. If decking or framing must be replaced extensively, we discuss with the lender and consultant whether that affects the loan type. Gutters, siding and window screens damaged in the same storm can usually be bundled into the bid.

faqs.q: Can I add a basement bedroom with a 203(k)?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Adding a legal basement bedroom usually requires an egress window, which may involve cutting into the foundation wall. That can be considered structural and point toward a Standard 203(k) with a HUD consultant. We assess the wall condition and layout so the loan type and scope are correct from the start. A properly drained window well is part of that bid, since a flooded well defeats the purpose.

faqs.q: Do you work with Wichita-area 203(k) lenders?
faqs.a: Yes. Any lender writing 203(k) loans in Sedgwick County can use our bids, and we adapt to each lender’s own draw forms and documentation rules. Many Wichita files reach us through a buyer’s agent who wants a contractor bid in hand before the inspection contingency runs out. Our part is the construction side: pricing, permits, scheduling, the work itself and the draw paperwork. Approval and oversight stay with the lender and consultant.

reo-renovation.title: REO Renovation Contractor in Wichita, KS | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Wichita REO and bank-owned renovations for servicers, banks and GSEs: hail and water damage, basement issues, code compliance, reporting.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in Wichita
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned and servicer-held homes in Wichita often arrive with a familiar combination of problems: hail damage that was never repaired, roofs leaking into ceilings, basements with water and wall movement, and electrical and plumbing systems that were already near the end of their life before the property went vacant. Servicers, banks, REITs and Government-Sponsored Enterprises need a contractor that can document these conditions accurately and bring properties to a marketable standard on a predictable budget. Government-Sponsored Enterprises list Genstone as a preferred contractor, and our leadership built its experience on bank-owned and REO work. For Wichita assignments, one field manager directs licensed local trades, carries permits and code items through MABCD and reports in the format asset managers already use, with Genstone Field Services covering preservation and recurring inspections.

sections.body:
Vacancy in Wichita tends to expose every weakness a house already had. A roof damaged by hail starts leaking into the attic and ceilings. Gutters fill and water collects against basement walls, which then crack or bow in clay soil. Sump pumps fail when power is cut or equipment is removed, and basements flood during spring storms, leading to mold and ruined finishes.

In winter, an unwinterized vacant home can lose supply lines, water heaters and fixtures to freezing, especially during extended cold snaps or ice storm power outages. Vacant properties also face theft of copper plumbing, HVAC equipment and appliances, along with broken windows and occasional vandalism.

We document each property’s condition with photographs and clear descriptions, separating immediate securing and safety work from repairs needed for marketability. That allows asset managers to choose the most appropriate disposition strategy with accurate information.

Slab homes and basement homes fail differently here. A slab ranch on the west side may only need roof, mechanical and cosmetic work after a vacancy, while a basement ranch a few streets over can need water removal, wall bracing and new finishes downstairs before it is safe to show.

Vacant properties in Wichita can draw complaints about tall grass, debris, open doors and deteriorating exteriors, and the city can issue notices requiring corrective work or perform abatement at the owner’s expense. Ignored violations can lead to fines and assessments that reduce recovery on the sale.

Our field services team keeps Wichita REOs ahead of those notices with routine visits: mowing, boarding broken openings, hauling dumped debris and logging each visit with photos. When a notice does arrive and the fix requires a permit, such as a sagging porch roof, exposed wiring or a failed foundation section, the permit goes through MABCD and the inspection result is added to the servicer’s file as proof of closure.

Addresses in Derby, Haysville, Park City or unincorporated Sedgwick County answer to different offices with their own notice periods. Each property in an assignment is tagged with its jurisdiction so a response never goes to the wrong desk, and the corrective work is built to that jurisdiction’s code rather than Wichita’s by default.

Wichita REOs rarely need the same treatment. We provide asset managers with several options: a stabilization package that secures the property, stops water intrusion and dries the basement; a marketable package that addresses roof, basement, mechanical and safety items so buyers can obtain financing; and a fuller renovation where neighborhood comps support it, typically on the east side or in College Hill.

FHA-ready repairs are particularly useful for entry-level Wichita homes, where many buyers use FHA financing. Addressing roof leaks, peeling paint, missing handrails and inoperable heating can widen the buyer pool and improve recovery.

All three tiers arrive as separate priced scopes, broken into labor and material lines with their own draw schedules, and hauling and dumpster fees sit inside each figure. Servicer and GSE files receive photo sets at intake, midpoint and completion, short milestone notes and trade lien waivers. Billing closes only after the work is finished and the asset manager signs off.

When an assignment covers many Wichita addresses, we rank them by exposure, so basement homes with failed sumps and open roofs are handled before slab houses that can safely wait a week.

faqs.q: Do you repair hail damage on REO properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Hail damage to roofs, siding, gutters and windows is common on vacant Wichita homes. We document the damage, provide repair scopes and coordinate licensed contractors to complete the work. If an insurance claim is involved, our documentation of conditions and completed repairs can support the servicer’s records. Temporary tarping is arranged first when the roof is open to the weather, so interior damage stops spreading while the claim is sorted out.

faqs.q: Can you handle flooded basements in vacant homes?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate water removal, drying, mold remediation where needed, removal of damaged finishes and repairs to sump systems and drainage. We also evaluate basement walls for movement, which is common in Wichita clay soils, and recommend structural repairs where appropriate. Each step is documented for the asset manager. We also check why the basement flooded, whether a dead sump, a clogged downspout or negative grading, so the same problem does not recur before the sale.

faqs.q: Can you take on a batch of Wichita REOs at once?
faqs.a: Yes. Servicers, banks, REITs, funds and GSEs often send us several Sedgwick County properties in one assignment. A single field manager runs the batch, so every address gets the same intake photos, scope format and reporting cadence. Properties are sequenced by risk, with active leaks, open structures and code notices first. That keeps the whole group moving while you review one consistent set of reports instead of several contractors’ formats.
